ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethical approval was obtained from the [BLINDED] University Ethics Committee.
Participants completed surveys before and after the summer and two diary surveys in between, approximately two weeks apart, so that experiences were reported within weeks of their occurrence.
Two hundred nonreligious British adults living in the United Kingdom were recruited through Prolific, with recruitment quotas for education.
Participants were aged 23-74 years (M = 43.4, SD = 11.5); 102 were men and 98 were women.

Twelve records contained no survey data (10 without a valid Prolific ID and two empty duplicates of existing participants) and were removed, leaving 200 participants who completed the pre-summer survey.
Participants provided informed consent at each wave and were paid for participation.
Next, we investigated how many participants had each of the experiences, see Figure 3 (and Table SM.2.3).
table.formatted: Next, we investigated how many participants had each of the experiences, see Figure <ref type="figure">3</ref> (and Table <ref type="table">SM</ref>.2.3).

table.text: In an exploratory analysis, we examined who the participants were with during their awe experiences.
Procedure Participants completed baseline and follow-up surveys six weeks apart, with two intervening diary surveys at approximately two-week intervals.
Participants completed surveys on 24 July, 7 August, 21

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 835 columns across 1 data file.
#### Issues Identified

41 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

**What this does not cover.** Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Participants completed surveys before and after the summer and two diary surveys in between, approximately two weeks apart, so that experiences were reported within weeks of their occurrence.
Two hundred nonreligious British adults living in the United Kingdom were recruited through Prolific, with recruitment quotas for education.
Participants were aged 23-74 years (M = 43.4, SD = 11.5); 102 were men and 98 were women.

Twelve records contained no survey data (10 without a valid Prolific ID and two empty duplicates of existing participants) and were removed, leaving 200 participants who completed the pre-summer survey.
Participants provided informed consent at each wave and were paid for participation.
Next, we investigated how many participants had each of the experiences, see Figure 3 (and Table SM.2.3).
In an exploratory analysis, we examined who the participants were with during their awe experiences.
Procedure Participants completed baseline and follow-up surveys six weeks apart, with two intervening diary surveys at approximately two-week intervals.
Participants completed surveys on 24 July, 7 August, 21

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 1 R code file.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1L, File = "Summer diary study of awe_R code.r", 
    "Runs after" = "—", Basis = "none"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited. **6 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 1 script: 0 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "Summer diary study of awe_R code.r", Outcome = "errored", 
    Detail = "undefined_variable", "Time (s)" = 4.5), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**Undefined-variable errors**

**1 script failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper's own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).


info.title: 42 Days of Summer: A diary study of awe

text.text: Awe has long been associated with religious experience, but it may also offer nonreligious individuals a route to transcendence, meaning, and wellbeing.
Most research has, however, relied on laboratory inductions and has treated awe as a single experience.

We conducted a pre-registered six-week diary study with 200 nonreligious British adults over the summer holidays, distinguishing three types of awe: transformative awe (being in the presence of something vast and mysterious that transcends one's understanding of the world), amazement awe, and reverential awe.
Over the summer, 78.8% of participants reported at least one amazement awe experience, 51.5% at least one reverential awe experience, and 20.6% at least one transformative awe experience.
The types differed in their contexts and phenomenology.

Nature was the most common context for all three, but transformative awe was more often related to space and religious, spiritual, or mystical experiences, and reverential awe to moral beauty and experiences with close ones.
Transformative awe was the most intense, followed by amazement and reverential awe.
Most experiences were rated as not at all religious (90.0%), but over half were rated as at least somewhat spiritual (52.5%).
The frequency and extent of awe did not predict changes in meaning in life, wellbeing, spiritual yearning, or spirituality from before to after the summer.
In exploratory analyses, the amazement rating of participants' most awe-inspiring experience predicted higher post-summer meaning in life and wellbeing.
These findings suggest that awe is not a single experience, and that nonreligious individuals frequently experience awe as spiritual but not religious.
Around half of British adults now report that they do not belong to any religion (Curtice, 2025).
text.formatted: Around half of British adults now report that they do not belong to any religion <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Curtice, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Nonreligion is, however, more than the absence of religion.

Nonreligious individuals endorse a range of secular beliefs and worldviews (van Mulukom et al., 2023), and some describe themselves as spiritual but not religious, although they understand this label in diverse ways (Wixwat & Saucier, 2021). Coleman et al. (2013) proposed that nonbelievers may experience horizontal transcendence, directed towards this world rather than towards a deity.

(2013)</ref> proposed that nonbelievers may experience horizontal transcendence, directed towards this world rather than towards a deity.

text.text: More recently, research has begun to examine spiritual yearning among nonreligious people, defined as a motivational state of longing for meaning, connection, or transcendence (Wilt et al., 2026).
text.formatted: More recently, research has begun to examine spiritual yearning among nonreligious people, defined as a motivational state of longing for meaning, connection, or transcendence <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Wilt et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This raises the question of which experiences might speak to such longings outside religious contexts.
In the present research, we examined awe as one such experience.

Awe has long been central to accounts of religious experience. Otto (1923 Otto ( /1970) described an encounter with the numinous as a 'mysterium tremendum et fascinosum', whereas James (1902 James ( /1988) ) argued that religious awe is the same emotion that people feel in a forest at twilight or in a mountain gorge.
text.formatted: Awe has long been central to accounts of religious experience. <ref type="bibr">Otto (1923</ref> <ref type="bibr">Otto ( /1970</ref>) described an encounter with the numinous as a 'mysterium tremendum et fascinosum', whereas <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">James (1902</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">James ( /1988) )</ref> argued that religious awe is the same emotion that people feel in a forest at twilight or in a mountain gorge.

text.text: Contemporary psychology is closer to James. Keltner and Haidt (2003) defined awe by two central appraisals, perceived vastness and a need for accommodation, and noted that it can be elicited by nature, art, and other people as well as by the divine.
text.formatted: Contemporary psychology is closer to James. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Keltner and Haidt (2003)</ref> defined awe by two central appraisals, perceived vastness and a need for accommodation, and noted that it can be elicited by nature, art, and other people as well as by the divine.

text.text: Awe increases religious and spiritual feelings (Van Cappellen & Saroglou, 2012), and recalling spiritual experiences increases awe through a sense of a small self in both religious and nonreligious individuals, with nonreligious participants more often reporting experiences in nature, science, and yoga (Preston & Shin, 2017).
text.formatted: Awe increases religious and spiritual feelings <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Van Cappellen & Saroglou, 2012)</ref>, and recalling spiritual experiences increases awe through a sense of a small self in both religious and nonreligious individuals, with nonreligious participants more often reporting experiences in nature, science, and yoga <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Preston & Shin, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Awe has also been associated with greater wellbeing and life satisfaction and lower daily stress (Anderson et al., 2018; Bai et al., 2021; Monroy & Keltner, 2023).
text.formatted: Awe has also been associated with greater wellbeing and life satisfaction and lower daily stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Anderson et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Bai et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Monroy & Keltner, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Its relationship with meaning in life is more complex, as the small self that awe evokes may also reduce a sense of personal significance (Rivera et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Its relationship with meaning in life is more complex, as the small self that awe evokes may also reduce a sense of personal significance <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Rivera et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Awe may therefore be well suited to sustaining a nonreligious form of spirituality, but whether the awe that nonreligious people experience in their daily lives serves this function remains unknown.

One difficulty is that awe may not refer to a single kind of experience. Keltner and Haidt (2003) proposed that additional appraisals of threat, beauty, ability, virtue, and the supernatural shape the character of awe, and threat-based awe differs from positive awe in its appraisals and its consequences for wellbeing (Gordon et al., 2017).
text.formatted: One difficulty is that awe may not refer to a single kind of experience. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Keltner and Haidt (2003)</ref> proposed that additional appraisals of threat, beauty, ability, virtue, and the supernatural shape the character of awe, and threat-based awe differs from positive awe in its appraisals and its consequences for wellbeing <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Gordon et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The everyday meaning of the word also varies.
In English, awe denotes amazement and wonder, but it also carries an older meaning of deep respect and reverence.

In our previous research with British adults (n = 206), amazement awe was associated more strongly with surprise, wonder, vastness, and beauty, whereas reverence awe was associated more strongly with respect, admiration, and self-diminishment [BLINDED].
text.formatted: In our previous research with British adults (n = 206), amazement awe was associated more strongly with surprise, wonder, vastness, and beauty, whereas reverence awe was associated more strongly with respect, admiration, and self-diminishment <ref type="bibr">[BLINDED]</ref>.

text.text: The two meanings were also linked to different contexts, with nature, music, and science associated more closely with amazement, and exceptional courage or kindness, moving speeches, leadership, and collective experiences more closely with reverence.

A third description comes from Keltner (2023), who asked participants in 26 countries about the feeling of being in the presence of something vast and mysterious that transcends one's current understanding of the world.
text.formatted: A third description comes from <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Keltner (2023)</ref>, who asked participants in 26 countries about the feeling of being in the presence of something vast and mysterious that transcends one's current understanding of the world.

text.text: Because this description requires that one's understanding be exceeded, it may capture a rarer and more transformative version of the epistemic awe that accompanies a revision of one's understanding (Gottlieb et al., 2018), which we refer to as transformative awe.
text.formatted: Because this description requires that one's understanding be exceeded, it may capture a rarer and more transformative version of the epistemic awe that accompanies a revision of one's understanding <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Gottlieb et al., 2018)</ref>, which we refer to as transformative awe.

text.text: Studies that ask about awe without distinguishing these meanings may therefore combine experiences with different psychological characteristics and, potentially, different consequences.
A second difficulty is methodological.
Much of the evidence on awe comes from experimental inductions using videos, autobiographical recall, or virtual reality.

These methods reliably elicit awe (Pérez et al., 2023) and allow causal inference, but the experiences they produce are brief and take place in artificial settings, and several prominent effects of induced awe have not been reproduced in recent replication attempts (Graziosi et al., 2026).
text.formatted: These methods reliably elicit awe <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Pérez et al., 2023)</ref> and allow causal inference, but the experiences they produce are brief and take place in artificial settings, and several prominent effects of induced awe have not been reproduced in recent replication attempts <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Graziosi et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Retrospective reports of past awe experiences avoid this artificiality but are subject to the distortions of autobiographical memory.
Diary studies offer a middle ground.
They have shown that awe is common in everyday life and is associated with daily wellbeing (Anderson et al., 2018; Bai et al., 2021; Monroy et al., 2023).
text.formatted: They have shown that awe is common in everyday life and is associated with daily wellbeing <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Anderson et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Bai et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Monroy et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, in a 22-day diary study, daily awe did not uniquely predict wellbeing at follow-up (Monroy et al., 2023), so it remains unclear whether naturally occurring awe is followed by changes that persist beyond the experience itself.
text.formatted: However, in a 22-day diary study, daily awe did not uniquely predict wellbeing at follow-up <ref type="bibr">(Monroy et al., 2023)</ref>, so it remains unclear whether naturally occurring awe is followed by changes that persist beyond the experience itself.

text.text: Few studies have examined these questions in nonreligious samples or have distinguished between types of awe.

To address these questions, we conducted a six-week longitudinal diary study with 200 nonreligious British adults during the UK school summer holidays, when people are more likely to travel, spend time outdoors, and break from their daily routines.
Participants completed surveys before and after the summer and two diary surveys in between, approximately two weeks apart, so that experiences were reported within weeks of their occurrence.
In each diary, participants indicated whether they had experienced transformative, amazement, or reverence awe, and described and rated each experience.
Our pre-registered hypotheses concerned three questions.

First, we expected participants to distinguish between the three types of awe, with amazement awe the most frequent and transformative awe the least frequent, and expected the types to differ in their contexts.

Second, we expected transformative awe to be characterised especially by a need for accommodation and self-transcendence, amazement awe by perceived vastness and self-transcendence, and reverence awe by self-diminishment and self-diffidence, and we expected some experiences to be rated as spiritual but few as religious.
Third, we expected the frequency and intensity of awe to predict increases in wellbeing and meaning in life from before to after the summer.
For spiritual yearning, we did not make a directional prediction.

Awe might increase yearning by drawing attention to needs for meaning, connection, or transcendence, or reduce it if those needs were met, and we therefore expected its relationship with awe to depend on participants' initial levels of yearning.
We also examined self-rated spirituality as an outcome and conducted exploratory analyses of participants' most awe-inspiring experiences of the summer.
Two hundred nonreligious British adults living in the United Kingdom were recruited through Prolific, with recruitment quotas for education.
Participants were aged 23-74 years (M = 43.4, SD = 11.5); 102 were men and 98 were women.
The data file contained 212 records.

Twelve records contained no survey data (10 without a valid Prolific ID and two empty duplicates of existing participants) and were removed, leaving 200 participants who completed the pre-summer survey.
Of these, 188 (94.0%) completed Diary 1, 184 (92.0%) completed Diary 2, and 167 (83.5%) completed the post-summer survey.
In total, 178 participants (89.0%) completed both diaries, and 160 (80.0%) completed all four surveys.
Participants who did not complete the post-summer survey (n = 33) had lower pre-summer wellbeing than those who did (M = 2.05 vs 2.45), t(48.2) = 2.98, p = .005.
They did not differ in pre-summer meaning in life (p = .22) or spiritual yearning (p = .39).
In line with the pre-registration, a missed diary survey was treated as missing, whereas a completed diary survey in which no awe experience was reported was scored as 0 awe.
In Diary 1, 140 participants reported at least one awe experience and 45 reported none.
In Diary 2, 111 reported at least one and 71 reported none.
Of the 178 participants who completed both diaries, 30 reported no awe experience in either.
Awe experiences.
Experiences were assessed for awe using the 12-item short-form Awe Experience Scale (Graziosi et al., 2024) Co-experiencers.
text.formatted: Experiences were assessed for awe using the 12-item short-form Awe Experience Scale <ref type="bibr">(Graziosi et al., 2024)</ref> Co-experiencers.

text.text: Participants indicated whether they experienced each event alone, with one other person, with a small group of up to 10 people, or with a larger group of more than 10 people.
These data are analysed in SM.4.
Wellbeing.
Wellbeing was assessed using the 14-item Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale (Tennant et al., 2007) August, and 4 September 2025 (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: Wellbeing was assessed using the 14-item Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Tennant et al., 2007)</ref> August, and 4 September 2025 (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1</ref>).

text.text: The first and final surveys assessed the principal outcomes, and the intervening diary surveys assessed awe experiences.

The diary surveys asked about three types of experience: (1) being in the presence of something vast and mysterious that transcends one's current understanding of the world; (2) awe as amazement, astonishment, or wonder; and (3) awe as admiration, deep respect, or reverence.
Participants indicated their frequency of each type (None, Once, 2-3 times, or More than 3 times), listed instances, and described and rated the most significant.
Reporting windows were the preceding month in Diary 1 and the preceding two weeks in Diary 2.
In each diary, participants first reported how often they had experienced each of the three types of awe: in the past month (Diary 1) or the past two weeks (Diary 2).
Those who reported at least one experience then briefly listed up to five experiences of that type, with the first listed as the most significant.
The number of text boxes shown depended on the frequency reported.

Participants then described the most significant (i.e., first-listed) experience in more detail, including its context, what triggered it, what happened, and what they felt or did, and rated this experience on the subsequent measures.
Surveys were administered through Qualtrics and took approximately 15 minutes each.
Participants provided informed consent at each wave and were paid for participation.
Ethical approval was obtained from the [BLINDED] University Ethics Committee.
Coding procedure
Coding.

We used Keltner's (2023) eight "wonders of life" as a starting point for the coding scheme, adding categories before coding on the basis of our previous research and during coding through an inductive process.
text.formatted: We used <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Keltner's (2023)</ref> eight "wonders of life" as a starting point for the coding scheme, adding categories before coding on the basis of our previous research and during coding through an inductive process.

text.text: We settled on 22 categories, see Table 1.
text.formatted: We settled on 22 categories, see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>.

text.text: Where an experience could be classified under more than one category, multiple codes were assigned, ordered by emphasis: the first code reflected the primary context of the experience, and any further codes reflected secondary contexts.
Where participants referred back to an experience they had described earlier in the survey, the coding of the earlier description was carried over.
Two coders (research assistants specifically recruited to this end) independently coded all descriptions.
Inter-rater reliability was assessed with Cohen's kappa, computed separately for each coding column with the irr package in R (Gamer et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Inter-rater reliability was assessed with Cohen's kappa, computed separately for each coding column with the irr package in R <ref type="bibr">(Gamer et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Because the order of codes was treated as meaningful, codes had to match exactly, including order, to count as agreement; the reliability estimates are therefore conservative.
Agreement was [moderate to substantial], κ = [range across context columns].
Disagreements were resolved through discussion between the coders until consensus was reached, and the agreed codes were used in all analyses.
For descriptive analyses, only the primary (first) code of each experience was used.
Identification of the peak awe experience.
Each participant could contribute up to six fully rated experiences: one for each of the three awe types in each of the two diaries.
To examine the consequences of participants' most intense awe experience, we identified a single peak experience per participant, regardless of diary or awe type.
For each rated experience, participants indicated where they would rank it on a scale from 0 ("no awe, an everyday experience") to 10 ("the most awe you have ever experienced").
The peak experience was defined as the rated experience with the highest score on this awe ladder.

Where two or more experiences shared the highest ladder score, the tie was resolved by selecting the experience with the highest rating of awe as a feeling of amazement, astonishment, or wonder (0 = not at all,4 = very much).
Remaining ties were resolved in a fixed order of awe type (transformative epistemic, amazement, then reverential awe), followed by diary (Diary 1, then Diary 2).
Ties occurred for 46 participants, of whom 16 were resolved by the amazement rating and 30 by the fixed order of awe type and diary.
Because each rated experience was the first-listed (most significant) experience of its type in that diary, the peak experience always corresponded to a first-listed experience.
Its context codes and detailed description could therefore be linked directly to it.
A peak experience could be identified for 145 participants.
Of these, 29 (20.0%) were transformative epistemic awe experiences, 97 (66.9%) amazement awe experiences, and 19 (13.1%) reverential awe experiences.
No peak experience could be identified for the remaining 55 participants: 38 reported no awe experiences in either diary, and 17 reported at least one experience but had no awe ladder ratings.
Analyses of the outcomes of the frequency and extent of awe included the 165 participants who completed both diary entries.
The peak experience analyses included all participants for whom a peak experience could be identified.
Missing data were handled by listwise deletion separately for each model, so sample sizes differ between analyses and are reported for each analysis.
In a further deviation from the pre-registration, connectedness is not reported here but in a separate paper [BLINDED], and spirituality was added as an outcome.
Religiosity was not analysed as an outcome because of a floor effect (pre-summer M = 1.06, SD = 0.28 on a scale from 0-4).

text.text: Nature was the most common context for all three types of awe.
Large-scale nature was over-represented for transformative awe (34.2%, z = 2.43) and under-represented for reverential awe (15.3%, z = -2.96).
Transformative awe events were also more often related to space (13.9%, z = 3.81) and religious, spiritual or mystical experiences (8.9%, z = 4.01).
They were less often related to close ones (5.1%, z = -2.36) or to witnessing great skill or effort (0.0%, z = -2.69).
Reverential awe events were more often related to moral beauty (9.0%, z = 5.51) and close ones (19.2%, z = 2.54), and less often to space (1.1%, z = -2.79).
Amazement awe events were more often related to mental stimulation (3.6%, z = 2.28).
They were less often related to moral beauty (1.0%, z = -3.90), mind-body practices or hobbies (1.2%, z = -2.29), and religious, spiritual or mystical experiences (1.5%, z = -2.02).

As predicted, participants rarely rated their awe experiences as religious, but often rated them as spiritual.
Of the 320 experiences (145 participants), 90.0% were rated as not at all religious (0), and none received the highest rating (4).

We pre-registered that awe experiences would increase spiritual yearning in participants with low presummer scores and decrease it in those with high pre-summer scores.
To test this, we added the interaction between pre-summer spiritual yearning and awe to regression models predicting postsummer spiritual yearning.
The awe predictors were frequency, overall AWE-S, and AWE-S for each type of awe, and all variables were standardised (n = 154 for frequency and n = 160 for the AWE-S scores).

None of the interactions were significant: frequency, β = -.01, p = .83; overall AWE-S, β = -.05, p = .33; transformative awe, β = -.10, p = .06; amazement awe, β = -.04, p = .49; reverential awe, β = -.03, p = .58.
The hypothesis was therefore not supported (Supplementary Materials).
The following analyses were not pre-registered.
We examined whether participants' peak experience, which was their most awe-inspiring experience of the summer (see Method), predicted the outcomes (n = 131).
For each outcome, we ran hierarchical regressions with standardised variables.
Model 1 included the pre-summer score and the number of rated awe experiences (1-6).
Model 2 added the amazement and reverence ratings of the peak experience.
Model 3 added the six AWE-S subscale scores of the peak experience (time perception, self-diminishment, connectedness, vastness, physical sensations, and need for accommodation).
The number of rated awe experiences was not associated with any of the outcomes.
The awe ratings of the peak experience explained additional variance in post-summer meaning in life, ΔR² = .021, F(2, 126) = 4.75, p = .01.
They also explained additional variance in post-summer wellbeing, ΔR² = .040, F(2, 126) = 6.71, p = .002.
In both cases, the amazement rating predicted higher scores (meaning in life: β = .12, p = .01; wellbeing: β = .19, p < .001), whereas the reverence rating did not (ps ≥ .11).

text.text: In this pre-registered diary study, we examined the awe that nonreligious British adults experienced over the summer holidays.
Participants distinguished between transformative, amazement, and reverential awe.
As predicted, amazement awe was the most frequently reported type and transformative awe the least frequently reported type.
The three types differed in their contexts and phenomenology, and most experiences were rated as spiritual but not religious.
However, neither the frequency nor the extent of awe predicted changes in meaning in life, wellbeing, spiritual yearning, or spirituality from before to after the summer.
In exploratory analyses, the amazement rating of participants' most aweinspiring experience predicted higher post-summer meaning in life and wellbeing.

Our findings support the distinction between different meanings of awe, extending our previous findings on the semantic associations of amazement and reverence (van Mulukom et al., in preparation) to experiences in daily life.
text.formatted: Our findings support the distinction between different meanings of awe, extending our previous findings on the semantic associations of amazement and reverence <ref type="bibr">(van Mulukom et al., in preparation)</ref> to experiences in daily life.

text.text: Nature was the most common context for all three types of awe, but beyond this, the types had distinct profiles.
Reverential awe was more often related to moral beauty and close ones, which corresponds with the older meaning of awe as deep respect.
Transformative awe was more often related to large-scale nature, space, and religious, spiritual, or mystical experiences, and was the most intense type on the awe ladder, the AWE-S, and the ESSS.

This is consistent with our proposal that Keltner's (2023) description captures a rarer and more profound form of awe, in which one's understanding of the world is exceeded (see also Gottlieb et al., 2018).
text.formatted: This is consistent with our proposal that Keltner's (2023) description captures a rarer and more profound form of awe, in which one's understanding of the world is exceeded (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Gottlieb et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Studies that ask participants about awe without specifying its meaning may therefore capture different experiences depending on how participants interpret the word.
Some of our predictions about phenomenology were not supported.
Self-diminishment and selfdiffidence were higher for amazement than for reverential awe experiences, and reverential awe experiences were rated lowest on the AWE-S and the ESSS.
Reverence ratings were also the only awe measure that was not positively correlated with the others, and they were unrelated to how spiritual an experience felt.
One possibility is that the meaning of awe in contemporary English is closer to amazement than to reverence, as also suggested by our previous findings (van Mulukom et al., in preparation).
text.formatted: One possibility is that the meaning of awe in contemporary English is closer to amazement than to reverence, as also suggested by our previous findings <ref type="bibr">(van Mulukom et al., in preparation)</ref>.

text.text: Measures of awe such as the AWE-S may therefore primarily capture amazement, and only partially capture reverence.
Future research could examine the phenomenology of reverential awe in more detail.

Most awe experiences (90.0%) were rated as not at all religious, but over half of the experiences, and over three-quarters of transformative awe experiences, were rated as at least somewhat spiritual.
Spiritual ratings increased with the extent of awe.

These findings are in line with previous research showing that nonreligious individuals also report spiritual experiences, particularly in nature (Preston & Shin, 2017), and with the proposal that nonreligious individuals may experience transcendence directed towards this world rather than towards a deity (Coleman et al., 2013).
text.formatted: These findings are in line with previous research showing that nonreligious individuals also report spiritual experiences, particularly in nature <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Preston & Shin, 2017)</ref>, and with the proposal that nonreligious individuals may experience transcendence directed towards this world rather than towards a deity <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Coleman et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: They also suggest that, for nonreligious individuals, the spiritual quality of awe does not depend on a religious framework.

Contrary to our predictions, neither the frequency nor the extent of awe predicted changes in the outcomes over the summer, and the relationship between awe and spiritual yearning did not depend on initial levels of yearning.
Pre-summer scores accounted for most of the variance in all outcomes, which suggests that these constructs were relatively stable over the six weeks.
Our findings are consistent with those of Monroy et al. (2023), who found that awe was associated with wellbeing at the daily level, but did not predict wellbeing at follow-up.
text.formatted: Our findings are consistent with those of <ref type="bibr">Monroy et al. (2023)</ref>, who found that awe was associated with wellbeing at the daily level, but did not predict wellbeing at follow-up.

text.text: They are also consistent with recent failures to replicate several effects of induced awe, including on life satisfaction (Graziosi et al., 2026).
text.formatted: They are also consistent with recent failures to replicate several effects of induced awe, including on life satisfaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Graziosi et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that the longer-term consequences of awe may be smaller or less general than previously assumed.
Across the sample, spiritual yearning and wellbeing decreased slightly from before to after the summer, whereas meaning in life, religiosity, and spirituality did not change.

Because the post-summer survey took place at the start of September, these decreases may reflect the end of the holiday period rather than the experiences of the summer, although our design does not allow us to test this.
The exploratory analyses of peak experiences suggest that what matters may be the strength of one's most awe-inspiring experience, rather than the number or average intensity of experiences.
The amazement rating of the peak experience predicted higher post-summer meaning in life and wellbeing, whereas its reverence rating and AWE-S subscale scores did not.
This is in line with the suggestion of Graziosi et al. (2026) that the intensity of awe may determine whether it has lasting effects.
text.formatted: This is in line with the suggestion of <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Graziosi et al. (2026)</ref> that the intensity of awe may determine whether it has lasting effects.

text.text: However, these analyses were not pre-registered, and the effects were small, and so they require replication.
Several limitations should be noted.
First, our design was correlational, and so we cannot conclude that awe experiences caused any of the observed associations.
Second, participants rated only the first-listed, most significant experience of each type in each diary, so the ratings may overrepresent more intense experiences.
Third, although the diary design reduced the time between the experiences and their reports, participants still reported experiences retrospectively, and Diary 1 covered a longer period than Diary 2.
Fourth, amazement and reverence were each assessed with a single item.

Fifth, the six-week period may have been too short for changes in relatively stable constructs such as meaning in life and spirituality, and future studies could follow participants over longer periods.
Finally, our sample consisted of nonreligious British adults recruited online.

Because religiosity showed a floor effect, we could not examine religiosity as an outcome, and future research could examine whether the same types of awe, and the same associations with spirituality, are found among religious individuals and in other cultural contexts.
In conclusion, awe is felt in a variety of experiences.
Nonreligious British adults distinguished between transformative, amazement, and reverential awe in their daily lives, and these types differed in their contexts, intensity, and spiritual quality.
Although awe was often experienced as spiritual, its frequency and extent did not predict changes in meaning in life, wellbeing, spiritual yearning, or spirituality over the summer.
Future research on the consequences of awe should take into account which type of awe participants experience, and how strong their most awe-inspiring experiences are.

text.text: We pre-registered that the four awe measures (AWE-S, ESSS, awe ladder, and the single-item awe ratings) would be highly correlated within any one experience.
Across experiences, AWE-S and ESSS scores were highly correlated (r = .83), and both correlated moderately with the awe ladder and amazement ratings (rs = .46-.50).
Reverence ratings correlated weakly with the other measures (rs = .05-.36).
Within participants (repeated-measures correlations, df = 174), the AWE-S correlated with the ESSS (r = .71), the awe ladder (r = .55), and amazement ratings (r = .55).
The ESSS correlated with the awe ladder (r = .51) and amazement ratings (r = .43; all ps < .001).

text.text: In an exploratory analysis, we examined who the participants were with during their awe experiences.
Most experiences were shared with others (69.4%): with one other person (36.3%), a small group (25.3%) or a larger group (7.8%).
The remaining 30.6% were experienced alone.
This distribution differed between types of awe, χ²(6, N = 320) = 13.58, Monte Carlo p = .035, Cramér's V = .15.
Almost half of the transformative awe experiences happened alone (48.9%), compared with 30.9% of amazement and 22.0% of reverential awe experiences (Table SM.4.1).
text.formatted: Almost half of the transformative awe experiences happened alone (48.9%), compared with 30.9% of amazement and 22.0% of reverential awe experiences (Table <ref type="table">SM</ref>.4.1).

text.text: Experiences shared with others were ranked higher on the awe ladder than experiences had alone (0.23 SD, p = .04), and received lower scores on the AWE-S connectedness subscale (-0.29 SD, p = .012).
These models controlled for type of awe and diary entry.
Being with others was not associated with AWE-S (p = .73), ESSS (p = .06), amazement ratings (p = .35) or reverence ratings (p = .36).

text.text: We pre-registered the following predictions.
Perceived vastness would be higher for amazement than for reverential awe.
Self-diminishment and self-diffidence would be higher for reverential than for amazement awe.
Connectedness would not differ between the two.
Need for accommodation would be highest for transformative awe.
The analyses followed the same approach as in the main text (Table S2).

text.text: Self-diffidence was computed from ESSS items 14-17 (small, insignificant, self-conscious, irrational emotions).
Items 18 (frightened) and 19 (ashamed) were excluded because of low item-rest correlations and floor effects (pooled α = .67; α = .60-.71 across diary entries and types).
Perceived vastness was higher for amazement than for reverential awe experiences, F(2, 218.66) = 17.75, p < .001 (0.39 SD, p < .001), as predicted.

In a deviation from the pre-registration, we predicted post-summer scores while controlling for pre-summer scores, rather than analysing change scores, and so Step 1 included the pre-summer score.
Step 2 added the AWE-S scores for each type of awe, averaged across both diary entries; types of awe that were not reported were scored as 0.
Step 3 added the amazement and reverence ratings for each type of awe.
The AWE-S scores did not explain additional variance in post-summer meaning in life, wellbeing, spiritual yearning, or spirituality (ΔR²s ≤ .015, ps ≥ .29).
The amazement and reverence ratings for each type of awe did not explain additional variance in any of the outcomes either (ΔR²s ≤ .032, ps ≥ .07).
Pre-
Hypothesis 3a.

The analysis had two parts (n = 127): (Part 1) Cumulative models: the change scores were regressed on the AWE-S scores for each type of awe (Step 1), followed by the amazement and reverence ratings for each type of awe (Step 2); (Part 2) Frequency: the change scores were regressed on the frequency index separately.
All variables were standardised.
